abstract: As publications and products on time series forecasting (TSF) proliferate, researchers face a growing burden of analyzing existing work. First, not all publications release code. For instance, only about 20% of arXiv TSF papers have a code link in the surveyed period. Second, released code also requires manual maintenance. Thus, TSF researchers must constantly adapt or implement existing works. However, independent implementations can differ in experimental settings and are difficult to maintain. We therefore propose to use AI agents for benchmarking TSF research and even supporting autoresearch, e.g., developing new TSF models. Yet directly applying existing coding agents, such as Claude Code and Codex, is suboptimal: prohibitive costs, limited scalability to large research projects (e.g., benchmarking), and lack of self-maintenance. To address these challenges, we propose TSFLab, a self-improving agent-agnostic “workbench” that equips compatible coding agents with shared resources and tools for low-cost TSF research and continuous maintenance of research resources. Our experiments cover reproduction, benchmarking, and new method development. In reproduction and benchmarking, TSFLab improves task completion by 20–163% and cuts fresh tokens per completed task by 11–66% across baselines. A pilot study of agent-driven method development also shows improved forecasting accuracy via TSFLab, with 32.8–73.6% fewer fresh tokens and 9.2–68.8% less development time than the other settings.

sections.body: Only about one in five of the 1,707 papers since 2020 provides a code link, and code releases grow much more slowly than papers (Fig. 1(a)). Libraries also lag: TSLib grew from 18 to 41 methods despite over 1,200 new papers since 2024, and it announced in April 2026 that it is no longer maintained. Agents can help, but two problems remain. Their knowledge depends on training cutoffs, and independent configuration produces different settings and incomparable results across agents and teams. The paper proposes TSFLab, a workbench that sits outside any agent so it can be reused across agents. It has four modules: a TSF-domain guide, a knowledge structurer, an experiment workflower, and a recursive improver.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Only about one in five of 1,707 papers since 2020 provides code, so agents face outdated knowledge and inconsistent settings.

sections.body: TSF libraries and benchmarks, including TSLib, BasicTS, TFB, NeuralForecast and GIFT-Eval, provide implementations and evaluation pipelines. However, agents must read library code to recover settings, and methods are added by hand. Research agents such as TimeSeriesScientist, TimeCopilot and MetaCaster orchestrate forecasters or tune training, so they produce forecasts rather than conduct TSF research. General workbenches such as ToolUniverse, Scientific Agent Skills and Biomni-E1 supply tools for general science or biomedicine, not TSF methods under declared protocols. Self-improving systems such as STOP and the Darwin Gödel Machine revise a single agent. The Recursive Improver of TSFLab instead improves the shared workbench by checking methods against papers and official code.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior libraries, agent systems and workbenches lack shared TSF evaluation protocols, and self-improving agents improve only a single agent.

sections.body: The workbench sits outside each agent and supplies domain knowledge, procedures and tools without changing the agent's model or harness. **TSF-Domain Guide** holds entry instructions and 17 task-specific skills that give steps, checks and pitfalls. **Knowledge Structurer** keeps a card for each method, dataset and unit at three levels (summary, card and source), and 263 methods reuse at least one shared unit such as RevIN. **Experiment Workflower** runs agent-declared experiments through one runner that checks configurations before training, splits data as configured, fits scaling on training data only and selects checkpoints on validation data. **Recursive Improver** checks usability, complexity and consistency before accepting new methods, units or fixes, and failed checks prompt revision and rechecking.
sections.heading: TSFLab
sections.headline: TSFLab gives any compatible agent four modules: domain guidance, structured knowledge, a unified experiment runner, and verified shared updates.

sections.body: Baselines are TSLib, the TFB benchmarking framework, and no workbench, all run with Codex CLI and GPT-6 Luna under identical prompts, data and budgets. Tasks are reproduction of four recent papers without official code, benchmarking of eight methods on the new ERCOT and Openmeteo datasets, and a method-development pilot on ETTh1 and Weather. Table 2 reports completion, time, tokens, calls and added code per completed outcome. TSFLab uses 0.434 M tokens per completed reproduction, the lowest value in Table 2 for that task. The paper states that six benchmark results were not accepted. Table 3 shows that removing the TSF-domain guide lowers reproduction completion to 3/12.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: TSFLab completes the most tasks, 12/12 reproductions and 42/48 benchmark results, against 8/12 and 26/48 without a workbench.

sections.body: The paper presents TSFLab as a shared TSF research workbench that leaves the agent's model and harness unchanged. It combines domain guidance, structured knowledge, reusable units, execution and verified resource updates. Across the evaluated tasks, it improves task completion and token efficiency and supports method development. The ablations show complementary benefits from guidance, resource organization and shared execution. Retaining source knowledge, implementations and experiment records lets new agents reuse verified results and repairs as agents and harnesses change over time.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: TSFLab improves completion and token efficiency and supports method development without changing agents, and it retains verified results for later agents.

sections.body: The guidance, resource descriptions and experiment interfaces are designed for TSF methods and evaluation protocols, so their effectiveness in other research domains is untested. Extending the workbench would require adapting resources and checks to each domain's tasks and conventions. Within the limited search time, method development has not produced a new method that substantially outperforms all leading forecasting models. The reported improvements therefore show support for the evaluated development tasks, not a broadly superior forecasting method. More effective search strategies and longer research cycles remain future work.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Results cover only forecasting tasks, and method development has not yet produced a method that substantially outperforms leading models.

sections.body: TSFLab records the sources, upstream licenses and reference revisions of the methods it incorporates. Datasets keep their original licenses, and all data are public numeric time series without personal information. Reviews document discrepancies between papers and code together with the chosen implementation. Results should be read under their recorded protocols, and benchmark rankings do not establish that a method is best across all settings. Coding agents execute code with network access, so their runs should remain sandboxed. Agent sessions and model training consume GPU time and API tokens, which the workbench reduces by sharing implementations. Section 4.2 reports these costs, and Appendix D gives the hardware and prices used.
sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.headline: Coding agents should run sandboxed with explicit authorization for external actions, and results should be read under recorded protocols.

sections.body: Appendix A describes the framework structure, the shared entry file AGENTS.md, and the 17 skills grouped by module. Appendix B gives example knowledge cards for PatchTST, RevIN and the ETTh1 dataset. Appendix C covers declarative TOML configurations, the command reference, budgets and research rounds, and the records used for comparable results. Appendix D gives the shared setup, with codebases pinned to TSLib at 4e938a1 and TFB at a0087ed, and NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPUs. It also lists the datasets, the four reproduction papers, the eight benchmark methods, the fixed protocols, the metric definitions, and the API list prices checked on October 13, 2026.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the 17 skills, knowledge card examples, command and budget details, datasets, fixed protocols, metric definitions and price assumptions.
